title: Play is work
hookLine: play is children's work, and adults need it too

lines: PLAY IS THE WORK OF THE CHILD.
cards: A small girl is building a tower of blocks on the kitchen floor. Her face is fierce. Her tongue is out.
When it falls, she doesn't laugh it off; she starts again, more carefully, at the base. Call her to dinner and she'll tell you, quite seriously, that she's busy. She is.
There's a saying, sometimes credited to the educator Maria Montessori: play is the work of the child. Somewhere between that kitchen floor and the office, the habit can get lost. Today: lila.

teach.b: First, the child's side. Watch a child at play and you see what this path has been calling work: absorption, practice, trying again after failure, learning the shape of the world with the hands.
Whoever first said play is a child's work, the point stands. It isn't a break from growing up. It's how growing up happens.
Second, a city full of play.

teach.h: BOYS AND GIRLS PLAYING IN THE STREETS.
teach.b: When the prophet Zechariah describes a Jerusalem restored and at peace, one picture he gives is this: "And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in the streets thereof."
Old men and old women live in those streets again, each with a staff in hand, the verse before says, and children play. Peace, in that picture, looks like a game in the street.

Third, the world as play. In Hindu thought there's a word, lila, which means play. The Brahma Sutras, an ancient Hindu text, ask a hard question: why would a God who lacks nothing create a world at all?
The answer, in paraphrase: like the play of someone who already has everything, not for need, simply for play. Some Hindu traditions see the whole world as divine play. Fourth, the adult's side.
Grown-ups easily treat play as a reward for finishing the real work, and the real work never finishes. But play does things work can't. It has no outcome to protect.
You can lose and nothing breaks.
For ten minutes, the watching, measuring part of us gets time off. That isn't laziness. In the small builder's words, it's being busy.

how: Adults who make room for play often set aside short, regular times for games, music, sport, drawing or play with children, and treat that time as protected rather than as a reward for finishing work.

games.q: the Brahma Sutras ask why a God who lacks nothing would make a world. what's their answer?
o: like the play of someone who already has everything.
games.why: in paraphrase: it is simply play, lila, not need. it's a surprising answer to a very serious question.

practice: Go back to a game you loved as a child, hide and seek, a ball against a wall, drawing, a made-up world in the yard, and remember where you played it, and who with. Notice whatever comes, without telling yourself what it should be.
Then let one small kind of play come to mind, a puzzle, a song, a silly drawing, something with no point except itself.

wordCard.voice: Lila. The Hindu word for play: some traditions see the whole world as divine play, not born of need. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: play. If someone calls you away from it, you're allowed to say you're busy. Day nine hundred twenty-nine, done.
